title: “Is your project stuck?”
lead: 10 questions, 3 answers each, 2 minutes. The score adds 0, 1 or 2 points per question: the higher it is, the more exposed the project.

labels.keyboard: With the keyboard: {keys} to answer, {enter} to continue.
labels.privacy: The score is computed in your browser. Nothing is sent or stored.

result.none: Nothing to watch: every answer is green.

checklist.title: The test, on paper
checklist.text: Tick one answer per question, add up the points, then read your level in the table.

questions.question: How much of your critical code is covered by automated tests?

answers.label: Most of it, and they run on every change
A few tests, rarely run
Very few, or none

advice.2: Start with tests on the critical paths (payment, sign-in, business flows) rather than aiming for full coverage. A minimal safety net changes everything when you need to change the code.
advice.1: Run your tests on every commit and deal with the flaky ones: a test nobody runs protects nothing.

questions.question: What happens when a developer pushes code?

answers.label: Build, tests and quality checks run automatically
An automatic build, but the checks stay manual
Nothing automatic: we check by hand

advice.2: First automate build, tests and lint on every pull request. A day of setup saves weeks of regressions.
advice.1: Add the quality checks (tests, lint, dependency analysis) to the pipeline so nobody has to think about them.

questions.question: How often do you release to production?

answers.label: Several times a week, without stress
Once a month or less, as a planned event
Rarely, and every release is a risk

advice.2: Shrink the size of releases and automate deployment with a one-click rollback. The fear of deploying comes from the size of the changes.
advice.1: Aim for smaller, more frequent deployments: every release should become routine.

questions.question: How long does it take a new developer to ship their first change?

answers.label: A few days
Two to four weeks
More than a month, or “it depends on who helps”

advice.2: A README that gets the project running in under an hour, a reproducible environment (Docker) and a guided first ticket shorten onboarding.
advice.1: Document “day one”: setup, the architecture on one page, conventions. The gain repeats with every new arrival.

questions.question: How do you live with technical debt?

answers.label: It is identified, prioritised and dealt with regularly
We know it, but never have the time
It slows down almost every new feature

advice.2: Make the debt visible (a prioritised list) and set aside a fixed share of each cycle to pay it back, starting with what slows you down most.
advice.1: Put the debt in the backlog with its estimated cost: what has a figure ends up being weighed.

questions.question: Where does the project's knowledge live?

answers.label: Documented and up to date (README, architecture decisions)
Partly, out of date in places
In a few people's heads

advice.2: Write down the architecture decisions (ADRs) and an overall diagram. One up-to-date page beats fifty outdated ones.
advice.1: Bring the documentation closer to the code and update it in the same pull request as the change.

questions.question: Are your estimates and deliveries predictable?

answers.label: Yes, we usually keep our commitments
With frequent slippage
Impossible to predict, deadlines blow up

advice.2: Split the work into smaller deliverables and measure the real cycle time: you only forecast well what you have measured.
advice.1: Track the cycle time (from idea to production) to see where work waits.

questions.question: How many production incidents in the last three months?

answers.label: Rare, fixed quickly and analysed afterwards
Several, fixed in a rush
Frequent and recurring: we are fighting fires

advice.2: Set up monitoring, useful alerts and blameless post-mortems. Every incident should lead to a lasting correction, not just a patch.
advice.1: Formalise the post-incident review: root cause, corrective action, owner.

questions.question: If your key developer leaves tomorrow, what happens?

answers.label: The team carries on without trouble
A big slowdown
The project stops

advice.2: Spread the knowledge: pair programming, cross reviews, documentation of the critical areas. One person leaving must not stop the project.
advice.1: Find the areas only one person masters and organise their handover.

answers.label: Systematic code reviews, recorded decisions
Occasional reviews
Everyone does it their own way, with no guideline

advice.2: Set a few shared conventions (structure, naming, mandatory review) and record the decisions. Autonomy works better with guardrails.
advice.1: Make code reviews systematic: they spread good practice and catch mistakes early.

levels.title: A healthy project
levels.summary: The fundamentals are in place. An outside view can still save you time on a few specific points.

offers.text: In a lighter form: an outside view focused on the few points to watch.

levels.title: Costly friction
levels.summary: Nothing is broken, but the team loses time every week. A few targeted actions can bring the delivery pace back.

offers.text: A factual assessment and a prioritised action plan on these points.

levels.title: A project under strain
levels.summary: Several signals point the same way: the project is exposed to a standstill, a major incident or a key departure. Better to act now.

offers.text: Take back control of a project that is slipping: stabilise it, then get releases going again.
Take on the Tech Lead role in the team, for the time it takes to get the project back on track.
